read.sections.0.heading.source: Start with what you can see

read.sections.0.text.source: When you look at an artwork, begin with what you can see. Name the colours, people, objects and any words. Notice the composition, which means how the parts are arranged. In the poster, a blue river runs through the centre. Three people carry buckets towards one tap, and a child points at a cracked pipe. These are observations. They are facts that anyone can check by looking. The words “Water for every street” are also part of the evidence. Only after you look closely should you decide what the artwork might mean.
read.sections.0.text.back: When you look at art, start with what you see. Name the colours, people, objects and words there are. Notice the composition, which means how the parts of the picture are arranged. In the poster, a blue river flows through the middle, three people carry buckets to a single tap, and a child points to a cracked pipe. These are observations, facts anyone can check by looking. The words "Water for every street" are part of the evidence too. You should decide what the art might mean only after looking carefully.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: First, look at what you can see. Name the colours, people, things and words. See how the parts are placed. This is the composition. A blue river is in the middle. Three people carry buckets to one tap. A child points at a broken pipe. These are observations. Anyone can check them by looking. The words on the poster are evidence too. Look closely first. Then think about what it means.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: First, look at what you see. Name the colours, people, objects and words. See how the parts are placed. This is composition. The blue river is in the middle. Three people carry buckets to a single tap. A child points to the broken pipe. These are observations. Anyone can check them by looking. The words on the poster are evidence too. Look carefully first, then think about what the picture means.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Art has told stories for a very long time
read.sections.1.heading.back: Art has told stories for a very long time

read.sections.1.text.source: People around the world use art to tell stories and keep knowledge. At Tassili n'Ajjer in Algeria, rock art shows hippos and herds of cattle. The land there is desert today, so the pictures tell us the Sahara was once much greener. In China, there is a painted scroll more than five metres long. It shows over 800 people shopping, travelling and working in a busy city about 900 years ago. It is called Along the River During the Qingming Festival. In Vanuatu, in the Pacific, sand drawers use one finger to draw one long line. Their drawings help people remember stories and knowledge.
read.sections.1.text.back: People around the world use art to tell stories and keep knowledge. At Tassili n'Ajjer in Algeria, rock pictures show hippos and herds of cattle. Today that area is desert, so these pictures tell us the Sahara used to be much greener. In China there is a painted scroll more than five metres long. It shows more than 800 people shopping, travelling and working in a busy city about 900 years ago. It is called Along the River During the Qingming Festival. In Vanuatu, in the Pacific, sand drawers use one finger to draw one long line. Their drawings help people remember stories and knowledge.
read.sections.1.text.note: Real names given Thai spellings that a native speaker should confirm: Tassili n'Ajjer = ตัสซีลีนาจแจร์ (the source label adds the Latin name in brackets), Algeria = แอลจีเรีย, Sahara = ซาฮารา, Vanuatu = วานูอาตู. The Chinese scroll "Along the River During the Qingming Festival" = ภาพริมแม่น้ำในเทศกาลเชงเม้ง (Thai writers also use ภาพริมแม่น้ำยามเทศกาลเชงเม้ง); the checker warns that "Qingming" is no longer in Latin letters, which is expected. "sand drawers" = คนวาดภาพบนทราย.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: People all over the world tell stories with art. In Algeria, old rock art shows cows and river animals. Now the land is desert. So the art tells us the land was once green. In China, a long painted scroll shows a busy city. It shows more than 800 people. They shop, work and travel. In Vanuatu, people draw in the sand with one finger. The drawings help them remember stories.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: People around the world tell stories with art. In Algeria, ancient rock pictures show cattle and animals that live in rivers. Now that area is desert. So the pictures tell us the area used to be green. In China, a long scroll shows a busy city. It has more than 800 people. They shop, work and travel. In Vanuatu, people draw pictures in sand with one finger. The drawings help them remember stories.

read.sections.2.text.source: An interpretation is an idea about what an artwork means. A strong interpretation points to details. Viewer 1 thinks the poster is about people who do not have enough water. The line of people at one tap and the words at the bottom support this idea. Viewer 2 thinks the poster asks the town to fix the pipe, because the child points right at it. Both ideas use evidence, so both can make sense. It also helps to think about the audience, the people the artist wanted to reach. Words like “may” and “might” show that you are being careful.
read.sections.2.text.back: An interpretation is an idea about what an artwork means. A strong interpretation points to details. Viewer 1 thinks the poster is about people who don't have enough water. The line of people at the single tap and the words at the bottom support this idea. Viewer 2 thinks the poster asks the town to fix the pipe, because the child points straight at the pipe. Both ideas use evidence, so both can make sense. Thinking about the audience, the people the artist wants to communicate with, helps too. Words like "may" and "might" show you are speaking carefully.
read.sections.2.text.note: The English hedging words "may" and "might" became “อาจ” and “อาจจะ”, which are close in Thai; the self-check and simpler text use the same pair. Check they still read as two cautious words a learner can use. Second pass: "both can make sense" had lost its hedge (ฟังขึ้นทั้งคู่, "both make sense"); now อาจฟังขึ้นได้ทั้งคู่, which fits the lesson's point about careful words.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: An interpretation is an idea about what art means. A good one points to details. Viewer 1 thinks some people do not have enough water. Many people wait at one tap. That is a clue. Viewer 2 thinks the poster asks the town to fix the pipe. The child points at it. Both ideas use evidence. Think about the audience too. Who did the artist want to reach? Use words like “may” and “might”.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: An interpretation is an idea about what an artwork means. A good interpretation points to details. Viewer 1 thinks some people don't have enough water. Many people wait at a single tap. That is a clue. Viewer 2 thinks the poster asks the town to fix the pipe. The child points at the pipe. Both ideas use evidence. Think about the audience too. Who does the artist want to communicate with? Use words like "may" and "might".

write.example.source: The poster shows three people carrying buckets to one water tap. I can also see a child pointing at a cracked pipe. This may suggest that some streets do not have enough water. I think this because many people share one tap, and the words say “Water for every street”. Another viewer might think the poster asks the town to fix the pipe. Both ideas use details from the poster.
write.example.back: The poster shows three people carrying buckets to a single tap. I also see a child pointing to a cracked pipe. This might tell us that some streets don't have enough water. I think this because many people use the same single tap, and the words say "Water for every street". Another viewer might think the poster asks the town to fix the pipe. Both ideas use details from the poster.

watch.summary.source: This is the same short video from Lesson 15. It comes from the Ayala Museum in the Philippines. This time, watch closely for details. The video shows a small green pot from China with two dragons on it. It shows a salakot, a wide woven hat, decorated with shell and silver. It also shows a small cloth with a poem sewn into it. Each detail is a clue. The dragons make the pot unusual, because most pots like it were plain. The shell and silver suggest that an important person owned the hat. The poem tells us how the cloth's owner felt. A careful viewer first says what they see. Then they say what it might mean, and which details support that idea.
watch.summary.back: This is the same short video as in Lesson 15. It comes from the Ayala Museum in the Philippines. This time, watch the details carefully. The video shows a small green pot from China with two dragons, a salakot (a wide-brimmed woven hat decorated with shells and silver), and a small piece of cloth with an embroidered poem. Each detail is a clue. The dragons make this pot unusual, because most pots like this are plain. The shells and silver hint that the hat's owner was an important person. The poem tells us how the cloth's owner felt. A viewer who looks carefully first says what they see, then what it might mean and which detail supports that idea.
